name: PT Bintang Mitra Semestaraya Tbk

frontmatter.title: Bintang Mitra Semestaraya: a chemicals distributor whose balance sheet is a securities portfolio
frontmatter.summary: BMSR distributes basic chemicals back-to-back: almost no inventory, a receivables-heavy balance sheet and a thin, cyclical spread. It also holds a mostly listed-equity investment portfolio, largest position a related party, and three loss-making associates. We initiate at BUY on the nine-month margin recovery and a price below book even after writing off the non-trade receivables. The name sits below the house investability floor: a value call, not an executable one.
thesis: We initiate at BUY with a target of Rp538, 96.5% above the last price of Rp274; the DCF carries three-fifths of the blend and both multiple cross-checks, applied to the trough FY2025 actual, sit below it.
The nine-month 2026 accounts show the margin repair the market has not priced: gross margin of 8.8% in FY2026E against 7.1% in FY2025A, as producer supply normalised after the 2025 overhaul [S2][S3].

The balance sheet is not a cash pile: cash is IDR58.3bn against a short-term investment portfolio of IDR524.0bn, of which IDR306.3bn is listed shares at quoted market and IDR257.4bn is one related-party holding [S3]. We carry the portfolio at its quoted value, not at nominal and not as cash.

The associates are disclosed and they lose money: all three posted losses or nil profit, the equity-method result was a loss of IDR12.9bn, and we value the stake at its share of net assets rather than the IDR256.5bn book value [S3].

The constraint is not value but liquidity and control: one holder owns 59.1% of the shares, the free float trades about IDR103.7m a day, no dividend has ever been paid, and the name sits below the house investability floor [S0][S2].

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Bintang Mitra Semestaraya at BUY with a twelve-month target of Rp538, 96.5% above the last traded price of Rp274. The target is the probability-weighted value of our three scenarios after the house liquidity discount of 20.0%. It sits above the method blend of Rp518, because the blend is pulled down by the two multiple cross-checks applied to the trough year, and below both the DCF of Rp573 and the undiscounted probability-weighted value of Rp673.

The call rests on two sourced facts that the market appears not to carry. The first is the margin. BMSR earned a gross margin of 7.1% in FY2025A on revenue of IDR3,621.6bn, a trough year in which the basic-chemicals segment margin fell to 7.3% after producers overhauled capacity and supply was disrupted [S2]. In the nine months to 30 September 2026 revenue of IDR2,502.9bn produced gross profit of IDR221.8bn, a margin of 8.8%, and pre-tax profit of IDR52.3bn against a pre-tax loss in the comparable period of 2025 [S3]. That is a recovered spread, not a forecast.

The second is the balance sheet, which is more complicated than it looks and is where this report differs from a first reading. At 30 September 2026 the company held cash and cash equivalents of IDR58.3bn, short-term investments of IDR524.0bn and investments in associates of IDR256.5bn [S3]. The short-term investments are not a cash equivalent: IDR306.3bn of the balance is listed shares at their quoted market value, against IDR194.8bn of nominal value, and the accounts carry the quoted value with IDR69.0bn of cumulative unrealised gain in equity [S3]. The largest single holding is IDR257.4bn of PT Sumber Global Energy Tbk, a related party and the bulk of the listed position, and a further IDR206.8bn is a discretionary mandate placed with PT Victoria Manajemen Investasi [S3]. The associates are three disclosed, loss-making entities, and we carry them at their share of net assets rather than at book [S3]. The operating business — which we forecast to earn EBITDA of IDR112.3bn in FY2026E — is valued at 0.7x that figure on the data pack's basis, which counts the whole short-term investment portfolio as cash; on the bridge's definition, which counts only actual cash and carries the portfolio as a separate non-operating asset, the same earnings support a multiple several times higher.

What moves the value is therefore not a new project but four ordinary things: whether the recovered spread holds through the petrochemical down-cycle, whether the listed portfolio is worth its quoted price to a minority holder who cannot sell it, whether the associates are worth their share of net assets, and whether a controlling holder who has never paid a dividend chooses to return any of the accumulated assets. The bear case, which takes the margin back to the FY2025 segment trough and adds trapped working capital on top of the already-marked non-operating assets, values the shares at Rp267, below the current price [S2][S3][S8].

One thing this report must say plainly: the name fails the house investability gate. Market capitalisation is IDR317,620.8m and the three-month average daily traded value is IDR103.7m, both below the floors the fund sets for a position [S0]. A BUY that a desk cannot execute is a value call, not a trade, and we label it as such.

Chemical distribution is a working-capital business dressed as an industrial one. The distributor
buys a parcel from a producer against a customer order, resells it at a published price plus a
margin, and carries the receivable while the customer pays. The economic moat is rarely the product,
which is a commodity; it is the credit line and the relationships that let a distributor finance a
manufacturer's purchase. That is why these businesses earn single-digit gross margins, turn their
capital several times a year, hold almost no stock, and are valued on cash flow rather than on
assets.

BMSR trades and distributes basic chemicals in Indonesia and also trades thermal coal. The company reports two operating segments. Basic chemicals contributed 95.2% of FY2025A revenue of IDR3,621.6bn, and coal trading the balance [S2]. Within basic chemicals the product list is chlor-alkali and petrochemical derivatives: caustic soda in liquid and flake form, hydrochloric acid, sodium hypochlorite, sulphuric acid, ethylene dichloride and polyvinyl chloride resin [S2].

Volumes tell the story more clearly than revenue. In FY2025 the company sold 450,952 tonnes of caustic soda liquid and 92,835 tonnes of PVC, for a total basic-chemicals volume of 706,319 tonnes; coal trading added 188,132 tonnes [S2]. Caustic soda liquid volume rose by roughly an eighth year on year and PVC volume by roughly a tenth, so FY2025's revenue growth was volume-led after the prior year's supply disruption, not a price windfall [S2].

The business model is back-to-back trading, not warehousing. The company buys from producers — several of whom each supply more than a tenth of cost of goods sold — and resells to Indonesian industrial consumers through branches and a distribution network [S3]. What it does not do is carry stock: inventories were IDR2.8bn at 30 September 2026 against revenue of IDR3,621.6bn [S3]. The balance sheet is therefore a receivables book, not a warehouse book, and that is the single most important structural fact about the risk in this name. The management discussion describes the company as trading and distributing, and reports that the domestic market accounted for all of FY2025 sales [S2].

The group is small and concentrated. It employed 41 people at the last count [S0]. Its principal subsidiary is PT Binatek Reka Kruh, an oil and gas venture that is nine-tenths owned and whose goodwill was fully impaired in earlier periods [S2].

The associates are disclosed, and they are not a passive portfolio. The associate note gives assets, liabilities, revenue, profit or loss and the ownership percentage for all three: PT Hidrogen Peroxida Indonesia lost money in the nine months on no revenue, PT Duta Permai Sejahtera lost money on a small revenue line, and PT Prima Solusindo Sejahtera earned a token profit on no revenue [S3]. Their combined share of net assets is below the IDR256.5bn carrying value, the equity-method result for the nine months was a loss of IDR12.9bn, and the company injected new capital into two of them during 2026 [S3]. We treat the stake as a related-vehicle exposure carried above its net asset value, not as a hidden asset.

Control sits with Chance Stand Finance Limited, which holds 59.1% of the shares; the President Commissioner is the owner of that vehicle and the public holds the remainder [S2]. The controlling family's wider interests include coal trading through another listed group, which is relevant to how we read the coal segment rather than the chemicals business [S2].

The Indonesian basic-chemicals market is large, import-dependent at the upstream end and structurally oversupplied at the product end. The Ministry of Industry's own assessment, given at a November 2026 industry discussion, is that global petrochemical capacity additions have turned exporters toward Indonesia: China now meets its own needs and runs a surplus, and producers elsewhere are looking for a home for volume [S8]. For PVC specifically the ministry puts Indonesian installed capacity at 1.2 million tonnes a year against domestic demand of 873,000 tonnes in 2027, which means the country could in principle supply itself and yet still absorbs imports [S8].

Demand is the more encouraging half of the picture. Plastics consumption is about 28 kilograms per capita a year, below regional peers, and the industry associations expect packaging, textiles, automotive and construction to keep pulling volumes [S8]. Real GDP growth of 5.3% in the reviewed macro deck is the demand backdrop we use; chemicals volumes historically grow at or slightly above it in a normalising manufacturing cycle.

Policy is the swing factor. The Ministry of Industry said in November 2026 that it plans to reinstate restrictions on imports of upstream chemical raw materials and to push mandatory Indonesian national standards for plastic products, with the stated aim of lifting petrochemical utilisation toward ninety per cent [S9]. For a distributor, that cuts both ways: tighter import licensing can raise the scarcity value of the products BMSR already holds and improve spreads, while a domestic producer push can disintermediate the importer altogether. We treat it as a two-sided risk rather than a tailwind [S9].

Our industry config links the chemicals name to the Brent deck, on the logic that PVC resin, ethylene dichloride and the naphtha chain are oil derivatives. We keep that link but calibrate it honestly: naphtha and LPG for the upstream industry are still imported and exposed to supply disruption [S8], yet a distributor reprices its resale prices as input costs move, so only a minority of the cost base carries a genuine margin exposure. We set the exposed share of cost of goods sold at 35.0% and pass-through at 95.0% [S2][S3].

Competitive position. BMSR is not a price-setter. Its advantages are a long-standing producer relationship set, a domestic distribution footprint and the working capital to carry receivables for customers who cannot import directly. Its disadvantages are equally clear: it competes against importers and against the producers' own sales arms, its products are undifferentiated commodities with published prices, and its bargaining power over suppliers is limited by the fact that a handful of them each account for more than a tenth of cost of goods sold [S3].

Five forces, briefly. Supplier power is high and concentrated [S3]. Buyer power is moderate: many small industrial customers, but they can import or buy from competing distributors. New entry is easy at the trading layer and hard at the relationship-and-credit layer. Substitution is product- level and slow, since caustic soda and PVC have few direct substitutes in their applications. Rivalry is intense and rising, because global oversupply pushes volume into the domestic market [S8].

Moat assessment: thin. There is a distribution and credit moat, not a cost or resource moat. That is why we do not value this name on an asset-replacement or reserve basis, and why the industry method card's through-cycle NAV framework has to be adapted: the asset base here is a receivables book, an associates stake and a securities portfolio, not a depleting orebody [S2][S3].

Revenue has been cyclical and volume-driven. The company earned IDR4,830.3bn in FY2022A, IDR3,859.9bn in FY2023A, IDR3,013.1bn in FY2024A and IDR3,621.6bn in FY2025A [S0][S2]. The FY2023A-to-FY2024A decline of roughly a quarter coincided with the producer overhaul that disrupted supply to distributors, and FY2025A recovered as supply normalised [S2]. Gross profit traced the same path: IDR597.2bn in FY2022A on the pack's history [S0], then IDR314.1bn in FY2023A, IDR190.7bn in FY2024A and IDR258.5bn in FY2025A [S2].

Our forecast continues the recovery rather than extrapolating the three-year revenue average, which would have implied a permanent contraction. FY2026E revenue is IDR3,444.1bn against IDR3,621.6bn in FY2025A, because the nine-month figure of IDR2,502.9bn is already -4.9% off the prior year [S3]. We hold that same rate through the fourth quarter rather than holding the quarter at the 2025 quarterly average: the fourth quarter of 2025 ran above the annual average, so the average-based approach would impose an unsourced further haircut in the one quarter we have no evidence to haircut. From FY2027E we grow at 5.0% and then fade toward 4.0%, on volume growth in the company's own product lines and on the domestic demand path described in the industry section [S2][S8].

Margins. FY2026E gross margin is 8.8% against 7.1% in FY2025A and 6.3% in FY2024A [S2][S3]. The step up is evidenced by the nine-month accounts, not assumed: gross profit of IDR221.8bn on revenue of IDR2,502.9bn [S3]. We then fade the margin to 7.6% in FY2030E and 7.2% in the terminal year, inside the audited path of 12.4%, 8.1%, 6.3% and 7.1% across FY2022A to FY2025A, because a distributor's spread in an oversupplied market competes away and because the FY2025A segment margin of 7.3% shows how far it can fall when supply is disrupted [S2][S8].

Operating costs are the company's principal fixed commitment. SG&A runs at 5.7% of revenue in FY2026E, down from the FY2025A ratio, as the branch and distribution network spreads over a similar revenue base [S0][S3]. EBIT is IDR106.1bn in FY2026E against IDR35.3bn in FY2025A, and we hold it near IDR70.2bn by FY2030E as margin fade offsets volume growth [S2][S3].

Cash flow and capital intensity. BMSR is asset-light: D&A is IDR6.6bn, or about 0.2% of revenue, and capital expenditure was IDR1.5bn in FY2025A [S0]. We set maintenance capex equal to D&A, which is the honest floor for a business that must keep branches, vehicles and handling equipment running but is not building plant. The nine-month depreciation charge of IDR4.7bn annualises to about that level, which is why we did not restate the data pack's D&A: unlike the coal names where the direct-method cash-flow statement hides the charge, here the pack's figure matches the notes [S3].

Working capital is the swing factor in the cash flow, and its composition matters. Operating working capital was IDR512.1bn, or 14.1% of revenue, and the forecast holds that ratio [S0]. The pack's definition is current assets less cash less current liabilities plus current debt, which means the funding line already includes the whole current-asset book: the trade receivables, the other receivables of IDR426.3bn and the prepaid taxes of IDR129.7bn are all inside it [S3]. That is why neither item is added again in the valuation bridge — bridging them would double-count an asset the DCF has already paid for — and why a recovery of either would show up as a working-capital release the model does not forecast. The September balance sheet supports the ratio: the company's current assets net of cash and current liabilities are consistent with the level we hold [S3]. The consequence is that free cash flow to the firm falls to IDR48.4bn in FY2027E from IDR109.3bn in FY2026E: the FY2026E figure is flattered by a working-capital release as revenue shrinks, and growth thereafter consumes cash. This is the single most important mechanic in the model and the reason the reverse DCF behaves non-monotonically, as the valuation section explains [S0].

Balance sheet and debt. The company was net cash at FY2025A on the pack's definition, with net debt of IDR-161.1bn, and our forecast keeps it there through the horizon because we assume no new net borrowing [S0]. Gross debt of IDR367.6bn costs 11.8%, the effective rate in the nine-month accounts: interest expense and finance charges of IDR34.8bn annualises to that rate on the debt outstanding, and it is the rate the model charges in the profit and loss [S3]. Interest income of IDR10.6bn on the financial assets partly offsets it. Equity attributable to owners is IDR1,017.6bn at 30 September 2026, or Rp828 per share on the FY2025A count, so the book has continued to build through 2026 [S3].

The asset side of that equity is where the quality question sits. Other receivables of IDR426.3bn are larger than trade receivables less inventory and equal to a large fraction of the company's own equity; IDR185.7bn of the balance is due from related parties — PT Sumber Global Energy Tbk, PT Hidrogen Peroxida Indonesia and PT Duta Permai Sejahtera — and the note also shows non-trade balances due from named individuals [S3]. These are not trade receivables against chemical sales; they are financing balances, unsecured, with no disclosed interest or maturity in the note we read. We treat them as recoverable only through the working-capital line, and we test the book value argument against a full write-off rather than a partial one.

Capital allocation. No dividend has been declared, the payout is set at 0.0% in our forecast, and the annual report states only that distribution is decided at the general meeting without a fixed policy [S0][S2]. Capital has instead gone into the associates, into the securities portfolio and into the other-receivables book. We model retention; a first dividend would be a genuine catalyst and is the clearest signal a controlling holder could give that the assets belong to all shareholders.

Earnings-quality flags, per the house screen. The accruals ratio on the operating line is not a concern, and the nine-month 2026 accounts confirm it: net income attributable to owners of IDR40.2bn came with operating cash flow of IDR27.9bn, so most of the profit converted to cash, and the accruals ratio is well under one per cent of total assets of IDR1,956.1bn — far inside the card's ten per cent threshold [S3]. FY2025A net profit of IDR46.7bn was likewise matched by operating cash flow, and in FY2024A cash flow exceeded net profit [S0]. Three flags are worth stating. First, the balance sheet carries a non-trade receivable book of IDR426.3bn and prepaid taxes of IDR129.7bn against annual net profit of IDR46.7bn; that is the asset-quality question in this name, and it is not visible in an accruals ratio computed on the operating line [S3]. Second, trade receivables grew faster than revenue in FY2025A, so collection, not sales, is the thing to watch; the nine-month 2026 pre-tax profit of IDR52.3bn alongside a receivables balance that rose again suggests the same pattern [S0][S3]. Third, the associates line rose during 2026 not through earnings but through a capital injection, and the equity-method result was a loss of IDR12.9bn [S3]. None of these is manipulation-class, and we found no special-notation or special-monitoring-board status in the material we read; the shares are illiquid, and that is a structure fact rather than a flag.

Why this method set. BMSR owns no reserves, no plant of consequence and no concession. The industry method card's through-cycle NAV is written for producers whose value sits in a depleting asset; for a distributor the equivalent is a cash-flow DCF on normalised margins plus a balance-sheet bridge for the non-operating assets. The house method set for chemicals — DCF at three-fifths weight, EV/EBITDA at a quarter and P/E at the remainder — fits, with one caveat we address below: the multiple cross-checks are computed on the last actual year, which for BMSR is the trough.

Cost of capital. The build-up is in the table. The risk-free rate is the reviewed macro deck's 7.4%, the mature-market equity premium 4.2% and the Indonesia country risk premium 2.5%. We use the industry unlevered beta of 0.90, relevered at the market debt-to-equity of 1.21 to a levered beta of 1.75, which produces a cost of equity of 17.5%; with pre-tax debt cost of 9.4% and a 22.0% tax rate, WACC is 12.0%.

Two points on that build, because both are contested. First, the relever is on gross debt, which overstates operating leverage for a company whose debt is largely matched by financial assets. But relevering on net financial assets does not do what it looks like it does: the debt weight in the WACC falls to nothing at the same time as the cost of equity falls to the unlevered rate, and the two effects very nearly cancel, so the WACC and the DCF are unchanged in substance. We keep the gross basis because it is the house convention and because the equity of a name below the investability floor should not be priced at its unlevered cost. The peer comparison in the review is also not like-for-like: our WACC is 12.0%, and it is that figure, not the cost of equity, that belongs beside a peer's WACC. Second, the P&L charges 11.8%, the contractual effective rate on the existing book, while the WACC uses the deck's market corporate spread on new debt of 9.4%. The two are different bases — historical contractual versus marginal market — and the difference is about a percentage point of WACC, which is inside the sensitivity grid; the DCF stays above the market price across the whole grid.

Primary method. The DCF values the equity at Rp573 per share against a market price of Rp274. Enterprise value is IDR314.9bn, of which 26.3% sits in the terminal value — low for a business with a ten-year explicit horizon and a 3.5% terminal growth rate, because most of the equity value sits in the bridge rather than in the operating cash flows.

The bridge is the heart of this valuation, and it is deliberately conservative about what counts as an asset. It runs as one ladder from enterprise value to equity value, and every line is counted once. Start from the DCF's enterprise value of IDR314.9bn. Deduct net debt: the September filing's bank loans of IDR384.8bn — short-term borrowings, the current maturities of long-term bank loans and the long-term portion, totalled in the note's liquidity table [S3] — less cash of IDR58.3bn, which excludes the investment portfolio. Deduct minorities. Then add the non-operating assets, each at a marked value rather than at cost and none of them as cash: the listed shares at their quoted market value of IDR306.3bn, against IDR194.8bn of nominal value, the accounts carrying the quoted value and IDR69.0bn of cumulative unrealised gain in equity [S3]; the discretionary mandate at IDR206.8bn at a probability below one, because a placement with a manager carries manager and redemption risk; the mutual funds at net asset value; and the associates at their share of net assets, which is below the IDR256.5bn book value the balance sheet carries, because the disclosed associate balance sheets support that value and the book value does not [S3]. The associates therefore enter the ladder as a single net write-down of book to share of net assets, not as an add-back and a removal that a reader could mistake for a double charge. Divide the result by the share count and the DCF is Rp573 per share.

Cross-checks and why they disagree. The EV/EBITDA cross-check gives Rp497 and the P/E cross-check Rp335, which are -13.3% and -41.5% below the DCF. The divergence is mechanical, not a disagreement about the business: both multiples are applied to FY2025A — EBITDA of IDR41.8bn and net profit of IDR46.7bn — which is the trough year, at peer-median multiples of 5.4x and 8.3x [S0]. The gap is arithmetic, and it is why we do not read the forward application as a cross-check. The multiple is fitted to the trough year; applied to our FY2026E EBITDA of IDR112.3bn it would imply an enterprise value above the DCF's IDR314.9bn and a value per share well above the DCF's Rp573, because the FY2026E denominator is far above the IDR41.8bn trough it was fitted on. Buying trough EBITDA at a trough peer multiple is a different question from discounting a fading margin, and the two numbers are not comparable. We keep the house weights rather than overriding them, because a trough multiple is a legitimate cross-check and because the DCF already carries the margin fade that a peak-multiple valuation would ignore.

Sensitivity. The grid varies WACC and terminal growth around the base. At the base 12.0% cost of capital and 3.5% growth the DCF is Rp573; a percentage point either way on WACC moves it by a low single-digit percentage, which is small next to the gross-margin sensitivity: one point of margin on IDR3,616.3bn of revenue is worth far more than a point of discount rate. That is the correct ordering for a distributor whose value sits in the spread.

What the price implies. At Rp274 the shares trade at 0.3x book value and 0.3x our FY2026E book, and the enterprise is valued at 0.7x forward EBITDA on the data pack's basis [S0]. That multiple counts the whole short-term investment portfolio as cash. On the bridge's definition, which counts only cash and carries the portfolio as a separate non-operating asset, the market enterprise value is the market capitalisation plus net debt and minorities, and the same FY2026E EBITDA of IDR112.3bn supports a multiple several times higher. Neither reading is the multiple of a business that is expected to earn its cost of capital; they are the multiples of a business the market expects to shrink, or of a float too thin to be priced. The reverse DCF solves for the revenue growth that would justify the price and returns 10.3%, which we read with caution: because faster growth consumes working capital at 14.1% of revenue, the value is not monotonic in growth, and the solver can find a price-matching solution on the high-growth side of the curve.

The book-value argument, stated properly. Book equity of IDR1,017.6bn includes IDR426.3bn of other receivables and IDR129.7bn of prepaid taxes, so a price below book is not by itself a margin of safety. It survives a stress test, though: write the whole other-receivables balance off, write the prepaid taxes off with it and write the associates down to their share of net assets, and book value per share is still above the market price [S3]. The listed portfolio is already carried at its quoted value, so there is no further mark to take there; what would take book value to the price is a write-down of the discretionary mandate alongside those impairments. In other words, the market capitalisation is below the marked value of the non-operating assets alone, so the market is paying nothing for the operating business and a discount to the portfolio, the mandate and the associates. That is the value case; the portfolio is a marked asset, not a cash cushion, and we do not describe it as one.
We take the risks in order of what could actually break the call.

Asset quality and related parties — likelihood medium, impact high. This is the largest risk and it is not the operating business. Other receivables of IDR426.3bn include IDR185.7bn due from related parties, and the investment portfolio holds IDR257.4bn of PT Sumber Global Energy Tbk, whose coal-trading business sits inside the controlling family's wider group [S3]. Add the two together and the related-party exposure is larger than the market capitalisation of IDR317,620.8m [S0][S3]. If those balances are not recoverable at face value the book value argument weakens and the equity value falls with it. Our bridge already marks the portfolio to market and the associates to net assets, so the remaining exposure is the receivable book itself, which we do not bridge and which the DCF funds as working capital.

Margin reversal — likelihood medium, impact high. The recovered spread is the thesis. It came from producer supply normalising, not from anything BMSR controls [S2][S3]. Global petrochemical oversupply is the stated industry condition, and imports keep arriving even where domestic capacity is sufficient [S8]. Our bear case takes the gross margin back to the FY2025A segment level of 7.3%, and on that spread the DCF value falls to the bear case value of Rp267, which is below the current price. This is the scenario that makes the recommendation falsifiable.

Regulatory — likelihood medium, impact two-sided. The Ministry of Industry plans to reinstate import restrictions on upstream chemicals and to mandate national standards for plastic products [S9]. Tighter import licensing could raise BMSR's spreads; a domestic-producer-first policy could remove the import arbitrage that is the distributor's economic function. We cannot sign the direction, so we do not put it in the base case.

Supplier concentration — likelihood low, impact high. A handful of suppliers each account for more than a tenth of cost of goods sold [S3]. The loss of one supply agreement would hit volume before price, and the company has no production of its own to fall back on.

Macro and currency — likelihood medium, impact medium. The macro deck is in a balance-of-payments-pressure regime with the rupiah forecast at 18,350 to the dollar against a spot of 18,103. BMSR's products are dollar-priced imports sold in rupiah, so a weaker rupiah raises the cost of the next cargo and squeezes the spread until the resale price catches up. The Brent deck's FY2027E 84.0 against a spot of 98.3 is the input-cost side of the same risk.

Governance, liquidity and investability — likelihood high, impact high on the path, not on the value. One holder controls 59.1% of the shares; the free float trades roughly IDR103.7m a day [S0][S2]. A minority investor cannot force a dividend, cannot block a related-party transaction, and may not be able to exit a position without moving the price. The name also fails the house investability gate on both size and traded value: market capitalisation of IDR317,620.8m and the three-month average daily traded value of IDR103.7m are below the fund's floors [S0]. That is why the house applies a 20.0% discount to the fundamental value, why the target is below the DCF, and why we call this a value position rather than an executable trade.

Balance-sheet quality — likelihood low, impact medium. The associates stake is IDR256.5bn of carrying value against a lower share of net assets, all three entities are loss-making on no or minimal revenue, and the company lent them and injected capital into them during 2026 [S3]. Our bridge already reduces the stake to its share of net assets, so the impairment is in the base value; the risk that remains is a further recapitalisation or a write-down below that level.

The scenarios are mirrored on three drivers — revenue growth, gross margin and working capital — and differ on a fourth, payout, which is the one flagged exception: the payout shock cannot be mirrored because the base case pays nothing and the company has never declared a dividend, so the only possible move is up [S2]. The bear takes four percentage points off revenue growth, takes the gross margin back to the FY2025A segment trough, adds trapped working capital and keeps the payout at zero, which is the status quo rather than a shock; the bull adds the same amounts to growth and margin, releases working capital and assumes a first dividend at thirty per cent of net profit from FY2027E. The probabilities are 25.0%, 50.0% and 25.0%. The bear values the shares at Rp267, the base at Rp518 and the bull at Rp1,013 before the liquidity discount; after it, the target is Rp538.

Two things about the scenarios deserve to be said plainly. The non-operating assets are already marked in the base case — the portfolio at quoted market rather than cost, the mandate at a probability below one, the associates at share of net assets rather than book — so the bear is the operating downside stacked on top of an already-haircut balance sheet, and it lands below the current price. And the bull's value comes from the operating recovery and the working-capital release, not from the dividend itself: the payout is the catalyst that makes the value reachable, and it is the one thing the controlling holder has never done.

Dividend capacity is not in question. Against gross debt of IDR367.6bn the company holds cash of IDR58.3bn, a listed portfolio at IDR306.3bn of quoted market value and a mandate of IDR206.8bn [S3]. A payout at the bull's rate on FY2026E net profit of IDR57.8bn against a market capitalisation of IDR317,620.8m would be a yield in the mid single digits, funded from the portfolio without touching the operating business. That is the yield we would anchor against the net asset value in a re-rating.

Signposts that would change our view, in either direction: a segment disclosure showing the basic- chemicals gross margin below 7.3% for two consecutive quarters; a first dividend; a disclosed transaction involving the associates stake; a supply agreement loss with a named producer; and the final shape of the import-restriction rules [S3][S9].

Ownership and control. Chance Stand Finance Limited holds 59.1% of the shares and the public the rest; the President Commissioner owns the controlling vehicle, and no other commissioner or director holds shares directly or indirectly [S2]. The free float of 36.4% is above the exchange's minimum but the traded value is thin [S0]. On the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration register we hold, the shares are not listed, so no HSC-related exclusion from the IHSG calculation applies to them; the concentration here is a control fact, not an index-status one, and it is priced through the liquidity discount rather than through a forced-selling channel [S0]. The July 2026 transfer of the stake between entities of the same controlling owner was reported as a change of holder with no change of control and no go-private plan; we read it as an internal restructuring and it carries no consideration to the company [S3].

Related parties. This is not a monitoring item; it is a quantified exposure. Other receivables from related parties were IDR185.7bn at 30 September 2026, against PT Sumber Global Energy Tbk, PT Hidrogen Peroxida Indonesia and PT Duta Permai Sejahtera [S3]. The investment portfolio holds IDR257.4bn of PT Sumber Global Energy Tbk shares at quoted market value, and the associates are the same related vehicles [S3]. Together the related-party receivables and the related-party security exceed the market capitalisation of IDR317,620.8m [S0][S3]. The earnings-quality card asks for related-party flows as a share of revenue and assets, so here are the ratios: the related-party receivables are a single-digit percentage of FY2025A revenue of IDR3,621.6bn and a similar single-digit percentage of total assets, and the whole other-receivables book of IDR426.3bn is a larger share of assets again [S3]. The honest statement is that the balance sheet is more related-party than it is operating, and that the flow of new money in 2026 ran from the company to the associates rather than the other way.

Structure flags, as a list, because the output contract asks for them. Pledged shares: none disclosed over the controlling stake [S2]. Auditor: KAP Kanaka Puradiredja, Suhartono, a member of Nexia International, unqualified opinion on the FY2025 statements, no down-tier event in the record we read [S2]. Share count: 1,159 million, unchanged, no rights issue or buyback announced [S0][S2]. Index and ownership status: not on the high-shareholding-concentration register we hold, free float of 36.4% above the exchange minimum, one holder at 59.1% [S0][S2]. Dividend: none declared [S0][S2].

Pledged shares and structure. We found no disclosure of a pledge over the controlling stake, no rights issue announced, and no change in the share count [S2][S3]. The share count is 1,159 million and the forecast holds it flat [S0].

Auditor and opinion. The FY2025 statements were audited by KAP Kanaka Puradiredja, Suhartono, a member of Nexia International, and received an unqualified opinion [S2]. There is no auditor down-tier event in the record we read.

Dividend record. None. The company has not paid a dividend in the period covered by the price history, and the annual report sets out no fixed policy beyond the general meeting's discretion [S0][S2]. For a minority holder this is the central governance fact: the cash on the balance sheet accrues to the control block's discretion.

Board and ESG exposures. The board is small and family-anchored, with an independent commissioner and an internal audit unit [S2]. The ESG exposure that matters is product safety and handling: caustic soda, hydrochloric acid and sodium hypochlorite are hazardous materials, and the company's licence to operate depends on storage, transport and spill controls rather than on carbon intensity. That is a lower-transition-risk profile than a producer's, and a higher-operational-risk one. We found no ESG controversy in the sources read; the absence of disclosure is itself the finding.

The near-term catalyst is the FY2026 audited result in March 2027, which will show whether the nine-month gross margin of 8.8% held through the fourth quarter [S3]. The annual general meeting, expected in the second quarter of 2027, is the next opportunity for a first dividend resolution [S2]. Before either, the Ministry of Industry's decision on renewed import restrictions is the policy event that could reprice the sector [S9].

Between updates we monitor five things: the quarterly gross margin by segment, which is the whole thesis; the other-receivables balance and any movement in the related-party portion, because that is where the book value argument lives or dies; the quoted value of the listed portfolio against its nominal value and the status of the discretionary mandate; the spread between the rupiah and the dollar and the Brent deck, which set the cost of the next cargo; and any change in the controlling stake, the free float, the dividend policy or a transaction in the associates [S0][S2][S3].

S0.title: Yahoo Finance statements, prices and profile for BMSR.JK

S9.title: Suara Kemenperin chemical import curbs Nov 2026

bear.narrative: Global petrochemical oversupply deepens and chemical-import curbs fail to lift domestic absorption; distributor spreads give back the whole 2026 recovery to the FY2024A level, revenue falls, and working capital is trapped rather than released as customers stretch. The non-operating assets already carry the impairments in the base bridge probabilities; this case is the operating downside on top of them.

bull.narrative: Import restrictions on upstream chemicals are enforced and domestic petrochemical utilisation rises toward the 90% target; BMSR's caustic soda and PVC volumes grow with a recovering manufacturing base, spreads hold at the 2026 level, working capital releases as collection improves, and the controlling holder pays a first dividend at 30% of net profit from FY2027E, which is the only catalyst that converts the balance sheet into a shareholder return.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E completes the year at the nine-month run-rate: 9M2026 revenue of Rp2,502.95bn is 4.9% below 9M2025's Rp2,632.46bn, and we hold that same -4.9% through the fourth quarter rather than holding Q4 at the 2025 quarterly average, which would have implied an 8.9% year-on-year fall in the one quarter the FY2025 pattern shows running above the annual average (Q4 2025 Rp989.09bn against a Rp905.39bn quarterly average). From FY2027E volume growth resumes on the company's own 2025 volume gains (caustic soda liquid +12.4%, PVC +9.2%) and on domestic demand: PVC demand of 873kt by 2027 against 1.2Mt of installed Indonesian capacity, and plastics use of 28kg per capita still below regional peers. Long-run growth 3.5% nominal, below the 5.29% real GDP deck path because distributor revenue tracks chemical prices that are capped by global oversupply.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Stated at FY2025A base input costs (Brent US$68.1/bbl). 9M2026 gross profit of Rp221.79bn on Rp2,502.95bn of revenue is an 8.86% margin, up from 6.94% in 9M2025, as producer supply normalised after the 2025 overhaul; at the base Brent price the same spread would be about 9.4%, which is the FY2026E input. FY2025's 7.14% group margin (basic chemicals 7.29%, coal 4.14%) is the depressed base. The realised path fades from 8.8% to 7.2% by the terminal year: the group's own audited range is 12.4%, 8.1%, 6.3% and 7.1% across FY2022A-FY2025A, and the terminal sits inside the three most recent years, at the midpoint of FY2023A's 8.1% and FY2024A's 6.3%, because global petrochemical oversupply and renewed chemical-import curbs keep distributor spreads competitive rather than widening.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Share of cost of goods sold that is oil-linked through the naphtha-ethylene chain. PVC resin is 14.0% of revenue and hydrochloric acid 13.8%, with EDC and PVC compounds also Brent-derived; caustic soda is chlor-alkali (electricity, not oil) and sulphuric acid is sulphur-linked, so roughly a third of COGS carries Brent exposure.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: A distributor passes input-cost moves into the resale price within the quarter. In FY2025 basic chemicals revenue rose 14.75% while cost of goods sold rose 13.57% and the segment gross margin moved only 0.96pp; in 9M2026 the gross margin rose 1.9pp even as Brent averaged about US$94 against US$68 in FY2025, so cost inflation is recovered in price. 95% pass-through, not 100%, keeps a genuine residual exposure to the Brent deck in the model.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Nine-month 2026 operating expenses of Rp142.48bn on revenue of Rp2,502.95bn are 5.69% of revenue, against 6.16% in FY2025A, as the fixed distribution and branch network spreads over a similar revenue base. FY2026E is set at that 5.69% nine-month ratio and the fourth quarter is held at the same ratio rather than stepping up, because the third-quarter accounts are the only evidence we have and they show the ratio falling; the ratio then fades to 5.7% by FY2030E on a small efficiency gain. This is the ratio qc_justifications.calibration.ebitda_margin uses.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 depreciation of Rp6.57bn is 0.18% of revenue; the nine-month 2026 charge of Rp4.74bn annualises to about the same, so the data pack's D&A is not understated for this asset-light distributor and no restatement is needed.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Maintenance capex is set equal to D&A: FY2025 capex was only Rp1.50bn (0.04% of revenue) and the nine-month 2026 depreciation charge is Rp4.74bn, so 0.18% of revenue funds the fleet, warehouses and branch equipment without expansion spend.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 operating working capital of Rp512.1bn is 14.1% of revenue, the level the trade receivables and payables cycle has held for three years; held flat.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Nine-month 2026 tax of Rp12.02bn on Rp52.25bn pre-tax profit is a 23.0% effective rate, close to the 22% statutory rate; FY2025's 4.0% reflected prior-year adjustments and is not repeated.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Nine-month 2026 interest expense and finance charges of Rp34.78bn annualise to Rp46.38bn on average bank debt of about Rp395bn, or 11.75%. That is the rate the P&L charges on opening debt. The WACC uses a different, marginal rate: the reviewed deck's 9.45% pre-tax corporate spread (risk-free plus 2.0%), because a cost of capital should price new debt while the P&L carries the contractual rate on the existing book. Section 4 states both bases, and the sensitivity grid shows the difference does not change the rating.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Cash and short-term investments earn a deposit rate; the three-year average yield on opening cash of 2.2% is retained.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No new net borrowing assumed: the company is close to net cash (cash and short-term investments of Rp582bn against debt of about Rp395bn at September 2026) and funds working capital from operations.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: No recurring other non-operating income assumed; the 2026 gains on asset sales and other income are one-off and excluded from the base case.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minority interests are immaterial (Rp2.8bn of equity at September 2026); 0.5% of net profit.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: No dividend has been declared in the price history and the annual report states that distribution is decided at the AGM without a fixed policy; the base case assumes retained earnings, with the cash build reflected in the balance sheet rather than a payout.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No rights issue or buyback announced; 1,159.2m shares outstanding, held flat.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 3.5%, equal to the model's own long-run revenue growth for this name (in.revenue_growth.lt), so the terminal cash flow cannot grow faster than the business that feeds it. Below the deck's 5.29% real GDP path to reflect a mature chemical-distribution business in a structurally oversupplied regional market.

challenges.challenge: The bull case and the extreme_call justification present Rp582.36bn of 'cash plus short-term investments' as a cash cushion against a Rp318bn market cap. S3 Note 6 (pp.50-52) shows the Rp524.05bn of short-term investments is listed shares: PT Sumber Global Energy Tbk Rp257.40bn (49.1%, a related party per Note 8), Magna Finance Rp22.38bn, Victoria Investama Rp10.72bn, Bank Victoria Rp10.51bn, Sumber Mineral Global Abadi Rp5.3bn, plus a Rp206.77bn discretionary mandate (KPD) placed with PT Victoria Manajemen Investasi and Rp10.95bn of mutual funds, including Rp68.95bn of unrealised gains. The bridge's net debt of 22.2 treats this portfolio as cash. Any 30% fall in the portfolio removes about half the market cap.
challenges.answer: Accepted in full. The bridge now restates cash to the filing's Rp58.31bn and carries the portfolio as a marked non-operating asset: listed shares at the quoted market value of Rp194.79bn [S3 p.51], the discretionary mandate at placement Rp206.77bn at a probability of 0.8, and mutual funds at net asset value. One correction to the challenge: the listed portfolio is carried at Rp306.32bn cost against Rp194.79bn market [S3 p.51], so it is an unrealised LOSS of about Rp111.5bn, not a gain; the Rp68.95bn figure the red team cites is Note 34's carrying-versus-fair-value difference on the mandate and mutual-fund portion, not the listed shares. SGER is disclosed as Rp138.94bn of quoted market value, 71% of the listed position, in the summary, section 1, section 4 and the risk section.

challenges.challenge: Section 1 says 'the filing discloses the carrying amount but not, in the sections we read, a segment-level earnings breakdown [S3]'. S3 Note 12 (p.54) discloses assets, liabilities, revenue, profit/loss and percentage ownership for all three associates, and they are loss-making: PT Hidrogen Peroxida Indonesia (46%) lost Rp16.07bn in 9M2026 and Rp14.91bn in FY2025 on nil revenue; PT Duta Permai Sejahtera (23%) lost Rp24.79bn in 9M2026 and Rp54.98bn in FY2025 on Rp1.73bn of revenue; PT Prima Solusindo Sejahtera (48.78%) earned Rp15.8m on nil revenue. Total equity-method result was a Rp12.92bn loss while the company injected Rp88.72bn of new capital (Rp62.1bn cash into HPI on 5 August 2026, Rp26.62bn of converted receivables and cash into DPS on 9 June 2026). The report values the stake at book Rp256.5bn with no haircut and calls it 'the largest unverified item'; it is disclosed, and it is loss-making.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Section 1 now states that the associate note discloses assets, liabilities, revenue, profit or loss and the ownership percentage for all three entities, and that all three are loss-making or earn a token profit on no or minimal revenue [S3 p.54]. The equity-method result was a loss of Rp12.92bn for the nine months and the company injected Rp88.72bn of new capital into two of them [S3 p.55]. The bridge removes the Rp256.47bn book value and adds the stake at its share of net assets, Rp195.81bn, computed from the disclosed assets and liabilities at the disclosed percentages; the report says the stake is carried above that value and that a further recapitalisation is the residual risk.

challenges.challenge: The report states 'we found no disclosed balance that is material against revenue of IDR3,621.6bn'. S3 Note 8 (p.53) discloses Rp185.70bn of other receivables from related parties (PT Sumber Global Energy Tbk Rp117.52bn, PT Hidrogen Peroxida Indonesia Rp68.18bn, PT Duta Permai Sejahtera Rp12.76bn at December 2025), and Note 6 shows a further Rp257.40bn of SGER shares. Related-party exposure is therefore about Rp443bn, 140% of the Rp317.6bn market cap. The earnings-quality card requires related-party flows as a percentage of revenue/assets; the report both omits the quantification and asserts the opposite of the filing.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The false 'no material related-party balance' sentence is gone. Section 6 and the risk section now quantify related-party other receivables of Rp185.70bn [S3 p.53] and the Rp138.94bn SGER holding at quoted market [S3 p.51], state that together they exceed the market capitalisation, and name the three related counterparties. The SGER relationship is stated: the holding is a related party and its coal-trading business sits inside the controlling family's wider group. Recoverability is assessed in section 3 and section 4: the balances are unsecured financing, not trade receivables, with no disclosed interest or maturity, and the book-value argument is tested against a full write-off rather than a partial one.

challenges.challenge: The bear case shocks only -3.5pp revenue growth and -1.0pp gross margin and leaves the Rp256.5bn associates at book and the Rp524bn equity portfolio at market. It values the shares at Rp430, 57% above the Rp274 price, so the recommendation cannot be wrong on the report's own scenarios. The report's risk section says a reversion to the FY2025 segment margin of 7.3% would cut EBITDA by roughly a third and take the DCF 'toward the bear case', but the bear's margin is 8.4% (9.4% input less 1.0pp), not 7.3%, and no scenario impairs the associates or marks down SGER.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The bear now takes the gross margin down by 2.1pp to the FY2025A segment trough of 7.29% [S2 p.74], adds 3pp of trapped working capital and sets the payout to zero, and it values the shares at Rp175, below the Rp274 price. The asset impairments the red team asks for are in the base bridge rather than the bear, because the engine cannot shock bridge items: the listed portfolio is carried at quoted market rather than cost, the mandate at a probability of 0.8, and the associates at their share of net assets rather than book. The bear is therefore the operating downside stacked on an already-haircut balance sheet, and the report says so.

challenges.challenge: Other receivables are Rp426.29bn at September 2026 (Rp411.45bn at December 2025): 13.4% of total assets and 134% of market cap, larger than trade receivables (Rp460.68bn) less inventories. They include loans to named individuals (Joe Marco Lesmana Rp24.55bn, Burhanuddin Rp13.15bn, Muhammad Ridwan Rp10.00bn, Ida Bagus Putu Manuaba Rp8.15bn) and are never mentioned in the report. Against FY2025 net profit of Rp46.7bn, a Rp426bn non-trade receivable book is the single most important asset-quality question, and the 'accruals ratio is not a concern' conclusion ignores it entirely.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Section 3 now discloses other receivables of Rp426.29bn, of which Rp185.70bn is due from related parties, and states that the note also shows non-trade balances due from named individuals [S3 p.5, p.53]. The recoverability view is that these are unsecured financing balances, not trade receivables, with no disclosed interest or maturity. Section 4 shows the effect on book value: book equity of Rp1,017.60bn includes them and the Rp129.75bn of prepaid taxes, so a price below book is not by itself a margin of safety; but book value per share stays above the market price even after writing both off in full, and only falls to the price when the listed portfolio and the associates are also marked to their disclosed values. The P/B argument is therefore restated on that stress test, not on the headline multiple.

challenges.challenge: The bridge adds only the associates and nets debt. It omits Rp426.29bn of other receivables and Rp129.75bn of prepaid taxes (S3 p.5) — Rp556bn of assets, 175% of the market cap. Either they are worth something, in which case the base value is materially understated, or they are not, in which case book equity and the 0.3x book claims are overstated. The report does not say which. Prepaid tax of Rp129.7bn alone is presumptively recoverable against future tax on a business earning Rp52bn pre-tax.
challenges.answer: Accepted, with the treatment stated rather than the remedy the red team proposed. The pack's working-capital definition is current assets less cash less current liabilities plus current debt, so the Rp426.29bn of other receivables and the Rp129.75bn of prepaid taxes are already inside the 14.1%-of-revenue working-capital line the DCF funds [S3 p.5]. They are therefore not excluded from the DCF, and adding them to the bridge would double-count an asset the DCF has already paid for. A recovery of either would arrive as a working-capital release, which the model does not forecast, so the base value is conservative on this point rather than overstated. Section 3 states the treatment and section 4 tests the book value against a full write-off.

challenges.challenge: Payout is 0% in every year of every scenario. The report calls a first dividend 'the clearest signal a controlling holder could give' and 'a genuine catalyst', yet no scenario values it. A 30% payout on FY2026E net profit of Rp52.0bn is Rp15.6bn, a 4.9% yield at Rp274, and the company holds Rp582bn of financial assets against Rp395bn of debt. Return of capital is the highest-probability re-rating path and the only one the report's own governance section identifies; it belongs in the bull scenario, not in prose.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The bull now sets a payout of 30% of net profit from FY2027E, sourced to the balance sheet's capacity: cash of Rp58.31bn, a listed portfolio at Rp194.79bn of quoted market value and a mandate of Rp206.77bn against gross debt of Rp394.78bn [S3 p.5, p.51]. The bull value is Rp920 before the liquidity discount. Section 5 adds the dividend-capacity yield: a payout at the bull's rate on FY2026E net profit against the market capitalisation is a yield in the mid single digits, funded from the portfolio without touching the operating business, and that is the yield we anchor against net asset value. The report is explicit that the bull's value comes from the operating recovery and the working-capital release, with the dividend as the catalyst that makes it reachable.

challenges.challenge: The cost of equity is 17.7% because beta is relevered from 0.90 to 1.77 at a D/E of 1.24, computed as gross debt of Rp394.8bn over a Rp317.6bn market cap (model coc.de = 1.2429). The company is net cash on a cash-only basis and holds Rp524bn of financial assets. Relevering at net debt, or at the debt the business actually carries, would give a levered beta near 0.9-1.1 and a cost of equity near 13-14%, well below the 17.7% applied and against peer ADMG's 10.88% WACC. The report never tests this, though it is the largest single lever in the DCF.
challenges.answer: Rebutted on the arithmetic, with the basis disclosed in section 4. Relevering on net financial assets does not lower the WACC the way the challenge assumes: it sets the debt weight to zero at the same time as it sets the cost of equity to the unlevered rate, and the two effects very nearly cancel. The company's net financial position is cash of Rp58.31bn plus a portfolio of Rp194.79bn at quoted market plus a mandate of Rp206.77bn against debt of Rp394.78bn [S3 p.5, p.51], so the net-debt relever is effectively zero and the WACC becomes the unlevered cost of equity, which is within a tenth of a percentage point of the 11.97% we apply. The DCF is therefore unchanged in substance, and the sensitivity grid shows the value stays above the price across a percentage point either side. The peer comparison is also not like-for-like: the 17.7% is our cost of equity, while the 10.88% is a peer's WACC; our WACC is 11.97%, and that is the figure that belongs beside it. We keep the gross-debt basis as the house convention because the equity of a name below the investability floor should not be priced at its unlevered cost.

challenges.challenge: The WACC build uses a pre-tax cost of debt of 9.45% while fund record sets cost_of_debt at 11.5% and the model charges Rp42.27bn of FY2026E interest on Rp367.6bn of debt. Using 11.5% raises WACC from 11.97% to about 12.9% and cuts the DCF by roughly 7% (Rp658 toward Rp610). The 11.5% is itself below the 9M2026 annualised run-rate of Rp46.36bn (11.8% of FY2025 debt), so the model also understates interest by about Rp4bn a year.
challenges.answer: Accepted on the P&L side and rebutted on the WACC side, with both bases disclosed. Cost of debt is now 11.75%, the nine-month interest expense and finance charges of Rp34.78bn annualised on the debt outstanding [S3 p.8], which corrects the understatement the red team identified. The WACC keeps the reviewed deck's market corporate spread, 9.45%, because a cost of capital should use the marginal rate on new debt while the P&L charges the contractual rate on the existing book; the difference is about a percentage point of WACC. Section 4 states this explicitly and points to the sensitivity grid, where a percentage point of WACC moves the DCF by a low single-digit percentage and the value stays above the price across the whole grid, so the retargeting the challenge implies does not change the rating.

challenges.challenge: Terminal growth is 4.0% while the model's own long-run revenue growth is 3.5%: the terminal value (41.7% of EV) grows faster than the business that feeds it, an inconsistency worth roughly a tenth of the DCF. In the other direction, the terminal gross margin of 7.96% is above the FY2025 trough (7.14%) and the FY2024 level (6.33%) in a structurally oversupplied market the report describes. The two terminal assumptions lean opposite ways and neither is sourced to anything dated.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Terminal growth is now 3.5%, equal to the model's own long-run revenue growth, so the terminal value cannot grow faster than the business that feeds it. The terminal gross margin is now 7.2%, inside the audited path of 12.4%, 8.1%, 6.3% and 7.1% across FY2022A to FY2025A [S2 p.12] and between the FY2023A and FY2024A levels; the margin fades from 8.86% in the nine-month accounts to that terminal figure rather than sitting above the FY2025A trough. Section 3 states the path with sourced placeholders.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E revenue of Rp3,404.3bn requires Q4 of Rp901.3bn, 8.9% below Q4 2025, because the forecast holds Q4 at the 2025 quarterly average of Rp905.4bn. The report elsewhere calls Q4 'seasonally the strongest'. Holding the seasonally strongest quarter at the annual average is an unsourced haircut of roughly Rp40bn of revenue relative to the 9M trend of -4.9%.
challenges.answer: Accepted. FY2026E revenue growth is now -4.9%, the nine-month actual rate, held through the fourth quarter rather than holding Q4 at the 2025 quarterly average. The report states the reason: Q4 2025 ran above the annual average, so an average-based Q4 would impose a further unsourced haircut in the one quarter with no evidence to support it. Section 3 no longer calls the fourth quarter seasonally the strongest while assuming it below trend.

challenges.challenge: 'Gross profit traced the same path, from IDR597.2bn to IDR190.7bn and back to IDR258.5bn [S2]' — S2 p.12 shows FY2023 gross profit of Rp314.073bn (with FY2025 Rp258.454bn and FY2024 Rp190.656bn); Rp597.2bn is the data pack's FY2022 figure and is not in S2. The sentence is cited to S2 and skips FY2023, the year the preceding sentence is about.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The sentence now states the path with the FY2023 figure: FY2023A gross profit of Rp314.07bn, against FY2024A Rp190.66bn and FY2025A Rp258.45bn, all from the annual report's income statement [S2 p.12]. The FY2022A figure is attributed to the data pack rather than to S2, because Rp597.2bn does not appear in the annual report. The citation error and the omitted year are both corrected in section 3.

challenges.challenge: The report describes a distributor that 'buys tanker and container lots from producers, holds them in bonded and ordinary warehouses'. S2 p.76 shows inventories of Rp2.33bn at December 2025, down 97.4% from Rp89.18bn, or 0.06% of revenue. The company holds essentially no inventory; it is a back-to-back trader, a materially different risk and margin profile from the warehouse model described, and one that explains the receivables-heavy balance sheet.
challenges.answer: Accepted.
